Hong Kong leapfrogs Dubai as No. 1 super-luxury housing market — but can it last?
article:
Hong Kong has overtaken Dubai to become the world’s largest market for super-luxury home sales, but the city’s reign could be short-lived as a local rally shows signs of cooling and mainland capital constraints threaten to undermine demand into 2027.

Hong Kong recorded 78 sales involving homes priced at US$10 million (around $12.8 million) or more during the third quarter of the year, which were worth a combined US$1.58 billion, according to a report by property consultancy Knight Frank published on Nov 13.

The amount narrowly beat Dubai’s US$1.57 billion total from 86 deals, after the Gulf emirate logged a steep fall in transactions amid the Iran war.

But the headline ranking masks a market that has cooled since the first half of the year, when strong buying activity helped drive a broader recovery in Hong Kong’s luxury housing market.

“November has been very quiet, and investment sentiment is not particularly strong,” said Eddie Kwok, executive director of valuation and advisory services at CBRE Hong Kong.

“Luxury homes depend heavily on market confidence, and we expect activity to remain subdued through the end of the year and possibly into early 2027.”

Kwok said several headwinds had emerged in the third quarter, cooling investor sentiment.

Volatility in technology stocks, concerns over interest rates and weaker sentiment in the equity market more broadly could make wealthy buyers more cautious about committing to expensive properties, he said.

The value of Hong Kong’s super-luxury home sales nevertheless rose 52% from a year earlier in the third quarter, despite the number of deals falling 16% from the previous quarter, Knight Frank said.

Sales over the first three quarters of 2026 were already 49% higher than the city’s full-year total for 2025, according to the report.

The rebound has relied heavily on mainland Chinese buyers, who accounted for 72% of primary-market and 68% of secondary-market luxury transactions in the third quarter, according to an earlier report by CBRE.

But China’s recent tightening of controls over cross-border capital flows could constrain some mainland buyers’ ability to purchase expensive homes in Hong Kong, according to a September report by local surveying firm Pruden.

The city’s wider residential market also cooled in the third quarter compared with the first half amid reports of tighter mainland capital controls and a slower pace of new launches by developers, Pruden added.

The controversy surrounding luxury development One Stanley has added another source of uncertainty.

An investigation into alleged construction defects at the project prompted banks to become more cautious in assessing mortgage applications related to the development.

The slowdown could also affect developers’ sales strategies.

Kwok said developers were likely to become more cautious about launching new projects as market conditions weakened, potentially limiting the supply of fresh luxury homes available to buyers.

Dubai, meanwhile, saw super-prime transactions fall 34% in volume and 28% in value in the third quarter compared with the previous three months.

The drop came amid heightened geopolitical uncertainty following the outbreak of the Iran war, with buyers becoming more cautious after several years of strong property demand.

title: IWG launches Humanly brand targeting healthcare and wellbeing practitioners
article:
Workspace solutions provider International Workplace Group (IWG) has launched a new brand targeting customers in the healthcare and wellbeing industries.

Called Humanly, it offers a range of specialist treatment and consultation spaces for medical, therapy, wellness, beauty and fitness practitioners. The spaces include private consultation rooms, therapy suites, treatment rooms, fitness studios and reception facilities.

The brand is positioned as a flexible office solution that allows practitioners to scale up and down as needed, with Humanly taking care of the property and administrative requirements involved in operating a practice.

The concept for Humanly was developed in response to “growing numbers” of healthcare and wellbeing professionals using IWG locations, the company said in a Nov 18 release.

“Humanly allows us to take everything we have learned about creating great places to work and build an environment specifically around practitioners and their patients,” added Christian Schmitz, IWG’s CEO.

To date, Humanly has signed 60 locations globally, with the bulk concentrated in European countries such as the UK, Germany, Spain and Italy.

The brand has also made its Southeast Asia debut with a Humanly location in the Philippines. The outlet, located at the Aurora Pacific Economic Zone and Freeport Authority (Apeco) Super Health Center in Casiguran, Aurora, opened earlier this year.

IWG plans to scale Humanly further, supported by growing demand for healthcare and wellbeing services. “To have reached 60 locations in such a short period of time is a strong start and shows the scale of the opportunity,” Schmitz said.

IWG currently has a global network of over 5,000 locations across more than 120 countries worldwide, through brands that include Regus, Spaces, HQ and Signature.

title: Orchard Road and suburban mall rents edge up despite weaker retail demand: Savills
article:
Rents at Orchard Road and suburban malls inched up in 3Q2026, even as islandwide demand for retail space stayed soft, which could widen the performance gap between stronger and weaker assets, according to Savills Singapore on Nov 18.

Islandwide net retail take-up was -226,000 sq ft, an improvement from -398,000 sq ft in 2Q2026. Vacancy held at 6.5%, helped by a net reduction of 215,000 sq ft of retail space in the Central Region.

The Orchard area was the only part of the Central Region to record positive net take-up, at 11,000 sq ft. Mall rents in the area edged up 0.4% q-o-q to $23.80 psf per month.

In the suburbs, net take-up turned positive at 75,000 sq ft, which helped lower vacancy from 4.7% to 4.4%, while rents rose 0.2% q-o-q to $15 psf per month.

Rents in what Savills termed as the “fringe area”, which covers locations outside the Central Area but within the Central Region, fell 0.7% q-o-q.

F&B operators continued to be under pressure, with more than 24,000 food shops competing for diners. Several brands have scaled back their presence or exited the market. For instance, bakery chain Cinnabon has exited Singapore, Japanese-style cafe Hoshino Coffee closed two outlets and Chinese restaurant group Crystal Jade ceased operations at four locations.

Sulian Tan-Wijaya, executive director, deputy head of private wealth, and head of retail at Savills Singapore, said competition for consumer spending is intensifying even though demand for space in Orchard Road remains healthy.

“Being located in a high-traffic mall per se does not guarantee success,” she said, adding that brands must keep evolving to build a regular clientele amid dynamic changes in consumer preferences.

Limited new supply could offer some support for occupancy and rents, particularly for well-located, quality assets. About 252,000 sq ft of net lettable area is estimated to have come on stream in 2026, while completions are projected at 264,000 sq ft in 2027 — these are well below the 2021–2025 annual average of 474,000 sq ft.

Supply is expected to pick up from 2028, with annual completions projected to average 677,000 sq ft between 2026 and 2030.

In the pipeline are the redevelopments of Tanglin Shopping Centre and Tanjong Katong Complex . Larger projects such as the retail component of Changi Airport Terminal 5 are expected to add further supply beyond 2030.

Savills forecasts rental growth of 1% to 2% for both Orchard Road and suburban malls in 2026.

Alan Cheong, the firm’s executive director of research and consultancy, said the retail market is becoming more polarised as spending concentrates among a narrower group of successful brands, so the quality of asset management will increasingly decide how retail properties perform.

“While prime Orchard Road and dominant suburban malls continue to demonstrate resilience, weaker retail assets may face greater challenges in attracting and retaining tenants,” Cheong noted.

title: SGX Next 50: 3 Dividend Stocks Quietly Buying Back Shares
article:
Institutions sold more Singapore shares than they bought in early November, but a handful of companies were on the other side of the trade.
Over the five sessions to 5 November 2026, institutions recorded net outflows of S$140.9 million, while 19 primary-listed companies bought back shares worth S$11.1 million.

(SGX: U11),

The size of a buyback only tells you so much; you also want to know whether free cash flow can fund it.
Can Raffles Medical afford its buybacks while profit falls?
Raffles Medical Group
, or RMG, is an integrated healthcare provider operating across Singapore, Greater China, Vietnam, Cambodia and Japan.
Its S$1.19 million buyback ranked fourth among the 19 companies that bought back shares that week.
Its latest results were softer, with revenue for the first half of 2026 (1H2026) slipping 6.7% year on year (YoY) to S$353.2 million.
Profit attributable to shareholders fell 9.6% YoY to S$29.0 million, weighed down by lower occupancy at its transitional care facilities and a 52.3% drop in finance income.
Cash flow, however, moved in the opposite direction, with RMG generating S$61.3 million of free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capital spending) in 1H2026, up 17.9% YoY.
It also repaid S$51.1 million of loans during the half and held S$262.3 million in cash with no bank borrowings as at 30 June 2026.
RMG did not declare an interim dividend, in line with its practice since FY2021 of paying a single annual core dividend.
Its FY2025 final dividend of S$0.030, paid on 22 May 2026, was 20% higher than the S$0.025 paid a year earlier.
Can Pan-United’s cash flow keep pace with its profit growth?
Pan-United Corporation
, or PUC, is Singapore’s largest ready-mix concrete supplier and bought back 100,000 shares for S$158,240 during the week.
Construction demand lifted its results, with 1H2026 revenue climbing 37% YoY to S$549.6 million and net profit attributable to shareholders rising 49% YoY to S$30.6 million.
PUC also raised its interim dividend by 50% to S$0.015, from S$0.010 a year earlier.
Cash flow was more modest, with free cash flow coming in at S$7.4 million, up from S$1.0 million a year earlier.
A S$26.0 million increase in trade and other receivables tied up cash as revenue grew.
As at 30 June 2026, PUC held S$86.2 million in cash against S$21.0 million of borrowings, excluding lease liabilities.
Demand looks set to hold, with S$31 billion of the S$47 billion to S$53 billion in construction demand forecast by the Building and Construction Authority for 2026 already awarded as at June 2026.
Management also flagged energy cost fluctuations and supply chain disruptions as ongoing challenges.
Why is UltraGreen.ai buying back shares as its guidance falls?
UltraGreen.ai is a Singapore-headquartered provider of fluorescence-guided surgery solutions, with indocyanine green (ICG) as its flagship product.
The company bought back 250,000 shares
for S$127,421 on 3 November 2026, while SGX separately reported that chief executive Ravinder Sajwan bought 250,000 shares on-market the next day.
For the nine months ended 30 September 2026 (9M2026), revenue from continuing operations rose 35% YoY to US$131.8 million.
US revenue climbed 35% to US$101.3 million, while Rest of World revenue grew 36% to US$30.5 million.
The US market has become tougher, with rival ICG products from Zydus Lifesciences and Provepharm entering the market, creating pricing pressure and changing how customers buy.
UltraGreen.ai now expects FY2026 revenue to fall below its earlier guidance of US$175 million to US$185 million, although it has not provided a revised figure.
Management also expects the US business to remain under pressure in FY2027.
The company has room to act, with US$214 million in cash and short-term investments and no borrowings as at 30 September 2026.
The company has also proposed a share buyback programme of up to US$30 million and a target of paying out at least 30% of net profit, excluding exceptional items, as dividends each year.
Dividends would be paid twice a year, subject to board approval.
UltraGreen.ai has applied for a tax exemption that, if approved, would reverse a one-off US$8.5 million tax provision booked in FY2025.
Investors should strip out any such boost when assessing future profit.
Get Smart: Ask what pays for the buyback
A buyback during a week of institutional selling can look like a vote of confidence, but the better test is whether free cash flow can fund it alongside the dividend.
RMG’s 1H2026 free cash flow and cash reserves give it plenty of room.
On the other hand, PUC’s S$7.4 million of free cash flow fell well short of the S$24.5 million it paid in dividends in 1H2026, making its receivables worth watching in the second half.
For UltraGreen.ai, the key question is how much the growing US competition will eat into the profit supporting its dividend target.
Check the next set of cash flow numbers before reading too much into any buyback.

title: 8 Investor Dos and Don’ts as the STI Heads South
article:
It’s official.
The
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) is in a correction.
Last Friday (6 November 2026), the index closed at 5,180, almost 11 per cent below its record close of 5,802 in early September 2026.
Just two months ago, the STI was setting records.
Today, the mood has turned.
If you feel uneasy, you are not alone.
In times like these, it’s easy to lose sight of what matters and what doesn’t.
With that in mind, here are eight dos and don’ts for my fellow investors.
1. Do know the odds of a correction …
A fall of 10 per cent or more is not unusual.
It is the norm.
Historically, the STI has fallen by 10 per cent or more in around eight out of every 10 years.
Source: S&P Global Market Intelligence, Yahoo Finance, WSJ, author’s calculation
Said another way, a year without a correction is the exception, not the rule.
Knowing the odds won’t make a fall painless.
But it should make it less of a surprise.
2. … but don’t mistake odds for timing
Here’s the catch: knowing a market correction will occur tells you nothing about when it will happen.
Legendary fund manager Peter Lynch once observed that far more money has been lost by investors preparing for corrections than in the corrections themselves.
Imagine you sold your shares when the STI hit a record high of around 3,900 on 10 February 2025 — its first in 17 years — convinced that a fall was overdue.
You would still be behind today.
Even after an 11 per cent drop, the index is still well above 3,900 — and that’s before counting dividends.
There’s a deeper emotional flaw to consider.
If fear of a 10 per cent drop makes you sell, that same fear will make it hard to buy back when the drop arrives.
More often than not, the investor who sells early ends up waiting for a lower price — and never acts on it.
3. Do keep an even keel …
Investing in a falling market is not just about which shares to buy, or at what price.
You may land a great bargain.
But if you lack the stomach to hold, you will be prone to selling at the wrong time.
As Lynch put it, it’s not brains that will help you beat the stock market, it’s your stomach.
Start with the basics.
Keep cash for emergencies.
Only invest money you won’t need for the next five years.
If daily price swings are costing you sleep, consider paring back to a level where you feel comfortable.
Here’s a thought: when investing, don’t optimise for performance. Optimise for a calm mind.
A calm mind makes better decisions.
And better decisions lead to better performance.
4. … but don’t beat yourself up for not selling
Looking back, September 2026’s peak seems obvious.
It wasn’t at the time.
Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman called this hindsight bias: once we know how events unfolded, we convince ourselves we saw it coming.
Documenting your investment moves will help.
As humans, we tend to misremember our past experiences, especially when they involve major events.
On this note, the past six years have been full of challenging episodes that can distort our memories and directly impact the lessons we learn.
Therein lies the issue.
If you remember the wrong things, you will draw the wrong conclusions.
Even worse, you will be applying these wrong lessons in the future over and over again.
5. Don’t watch the scoreboard …
Warren Buffett once said that games are won by players who focus on the playing field, not by those whose eyes are glued to the scoreboard.
In a correction, the scoreboard — in this case, falling stock prices — is hard to ignore.
Every red number feels like a verdict on your investments.
But a falling share price only tells you how other investors feel.
It says little about how the business is doing.
Here’s a simple fix: remove the daily price-change column from your portfolio tracker.
6. … but do watch the business
A share price is made of two things: the business, and the mood of the market.
In a correction, the market’s mood does all the moving.
Prices swing on headlines and fear.
In contrast, business developments move at a slower pace.
They show up in what a company actually earns, quarter after quarter, year after year.
Lynch saw the same pattern.
Measured in months, he said, there is little link between a company’s results and its share price.
Measured over many years, the link is close to perfect.
So when the results come in, ask one question: is the business still growing?
One quarter shouldn’t change your mind.
A trend over several quarters might.
If the business keeps growing, a lower share price is not a threat.
It may well be a gift.
7. Do have a shopping list …
A correction is a good time to list the businesses you want to own for years, not months.
Keep in mind: you should buy because you want to own the business, not because the share price is lower.
Then decide how you will put your money to work.
Here’s a rule of thumb: take at least half as long to invest your money as it took you to save it.
If you took four years to save S$10,000, there is nothing wrong with taking two years to invest it.
8. … but don’t wait for the perfect price
In March 2020, Citibank’s research team downgraded
DBS Group
(SGX: D05) to “sell”, saying the shares were worth just S$17.50 — or S$15.90 after adjusting for DBS’s 2024 bonus issue.
I bought shares at S$18.40, above Citi’s target.
Today, DBS trades at just under S$70. My shares are up about 280 per cent, before dividends.
The lesson? You don’t need to get the perfect price.
Waiting for a “cheap” price comes with a catch.
Over the past 20 years, DBS has traded at one times book value only three times: during the Global Financial Crisis in 2008, the oil price crash in 2014, and the pandemic in 2020.
Each time, something had to go badly wrong first.
Get Smart: The opportunity you only see in hindsight
After almost two decades of investing, here’s what I’ve learnt: every past market decline looks like an opportunity.
Every future decline looks like a risk.
Looking back, buying DBS at S$18.40 in March 2020 seems like an easy call.
It wasn’t.
Four months later, the Monetary Authority of Singapore asked the local banks to cap their dividends at 60 per cent of the previous year’s level.
Vaccines were still just a hope.
Today’s correction will likely be no different.
A few years from now, it may look like an obvious opportunity.
Right now, it feels like a risk.
That’s why the dos and don’ts matter.
Know the odds, keep your calm, watch the business, and buy what you want to own, a little at a time.
As Charlie Munger, Buffett’s long-time business partner, said, the big money is not in the buying or selling, but in the waiting.

title: What is a Dividend? A Beginner’s Guide to Passive Income in Singapore
article:
Ever wondered how you can earn extra income without working extra hours?
Taking your first step into investing can feel overwhelming, but building passive income is simpler than you think.
Dividend investing
lets you become a co-owner in successful companies that share their cash profits directly with you.
Over the next four weeks, The Smart Investor is breaking down everything you need to know.
Whether you are new to investing or preparing for a secure retirement, we are here to help you take those first confident steps toward long-term wealth.
What Is a Dividend and How Does It Work?
A dividend is a payment that a company makes to its shareholders, usually from its profits.
In Singapore, investors can earn dividend income by owning shares in dividend-paying companies listed on the Singapore Exchange (SGX).
Take the familiar heartland supermarket operator
Sheng Siong Group
(SGX: OV8) as an example.
Suppose you purchased 1,000 shares of the company.
In the financial year ended 31 December 2026 (FY2026), Sheng Siong paid a dividend of S$0.07 per share.
That means, as a shareholder, you would have received S$70 in dividends.
But that is not all.
There are two ways to earn money when you buy shares:
Dividends: Cash received from owning shares.
Capital gains: Profit earned when shares are sold at a higher price than their purchase price.
But it is important to remember that dividends are not guaranteed, and share prices can also rise or fall regardless of dividend payments.
Why Do Companies Pay Dividends?
When a company turns a profit, there are a few things they can do with that cash.
One, they can reinvest in the business to support future growth.
Two, they can use these earnings to pay down debt.
Established companies with stable businesses often generate predictable cash flow, frequently more than they need to reinvest.
These companies may choose the third option: pay regular dividends to return that surplus to shareholders.
This can signal the company’s financial strength and boost shareholders’ confidence in future earnings.
Familiar names such as
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05),
Singapore Telecommunications Limited
(SGX: Z74), or Singtel, and
Singapore Exchange Limited
(SGX: S68) are examples of established companies with
regular dividend payouts
.
However, not all companies pay dividends and paying dividends does not automatically make a company a good investment.
How Much Passive Income Can You Get From Dividends?
A good place to start is the dividend yield, which is calculated as the annual dividend per share divided by the share price, expressed as a percentage.
If you invested S$10,000 in a stock with an annual dividend yield of 3%, that will translate to S$300 a year in dividends.

Investors can buy shares in Singapore-listed companies on SGX.
Two common categories of dividend-paying investments are:
Blue-chip stocks
: Companies with  long operating histories, strong reputations and consistent financial performance that tend to pay regular dividends, such as DBS and Singtel.

What Can You Do With the Dividends You Receive?

No investment is 100% risk-free.

Finally, high yields may look attractive but they can also be red flags in a business.
It may signal that a company is paying out more than it can afford – or that its stock price has tumbled due to underlying business troubles, pushing its yield up.
Before you invest, take the time to understand the business behind the dividend: how it makes money, whether its earnings are stable and whether it generates enough cash to keep paying shareholders.

title: Japan's Rakuten Bank shares tank as securities arm faces data breach
article:
(Nov 18): Rakuten Bank Ltd shares tumbled to their daily lower limit after the Japanese online lender’s securities unit said client data including names, addresses, annual income and financial assets may have been leaked.

The stock sank 19% in heavy trading on Wednesday in Tokyo, the biggest intraday decline since its 2023 listing. Parent Rakuten Group Inc slid as much as 7.5% to the lowest level in more than two years.

Up to 11.25 million accounts are at risk of having login IDs and client-specific codes breached, while personal data including birthdates and assets may have been leaked for up to 4.47 million accounts after suffering unauthorised access on Monday, Rakuten Securities Inc said in a statement on Tuesday. However, credentials needed for logging in and executing transactions were not compromised in the breach, which related to its test-environment system, the firm added.

For Rakuten Securities, “one emerging reputational issue is how such extensive client information was protected in a system used to test software or changes”, Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Michael Makdad said. “The question is why identifiable customer information was held there and whether it had adequate protection.”

A raft of companies around the world have suffered breaches or technical issues recently. In the US, JPMorgan Chase & Co faced a disruption to its system that slowed transactions this week. In Japan, financial firms ranging from SMBC Nikko Securities Inc to Daiwa Securities Group Inc have reported data leaks in the past few weeks.

See also: Japan to launch natural disaster warning network across Asia

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi announced an emergency cybersecurity package this month, which would include the use of artificial intelligence to strengthen basic protection measures and responses to cyberattacks.

Cybersecurity spending across the financial sector will clearly rise further, Makdad said. “The banking groups that can afford to win the cybersecurity arms race may be in a stronger competitive position at the end. It puts pressure on smaller groups that can’t afford to invest in the protection that will be needed.”

Shares of both Rakuten Bank and Rakuten Group have dropped more than 30% this year, compared with the broader Topix index’s 12% gain. Rakuten Group, an internet and telecommunications conglomerate, has struggled to recover from losses in its mobile business. Rakuten Bank is trying to achieve synergies after incorporating the securities and card businesses.

title: PM Wong expects ‘some impact’ from US chip curbs
article:
(Nov 18): Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said he expects some impact on the transhipment volume of high-end chips that flow through the city state as a result of tighter rules from the US.

“There will be some impact,” he told reporters on Tuesday in Manila following a regional summit, “but I think we can manage that impact. What we are more concerned about, of course, would be the chips that come into Singapore and are used by Singapore companies, by our data centres.”

Data centre operators in Singapore as well as Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will need a US government licence to purchase advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips from Nvidia Corp and other American manufacturers as they present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion”. The move threatens to put a damper on Southeast Asia’s boom in data centres housing the semiconductors needed to train and develop AI models.

Wong’s remarks followed a Tuesday meeting between Southeast Asian leaders and Donald Trump, during which Wong — seated next to the US president at a dinner — was seen laughing and engaging in lively conversation. The diplomatic bonhomie came against a tense backdrop, with Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow telling Bloomberg Television that Washington’s new restrictions on high-end semiconductor exports risk denting the region’s ambitions to become a major hub for data centres.

“If the US has concerns about how these chips in Singapore are being used, as we have said before, we can facilitate checks by the US government on companies in Singapore and how the chips are deployed,” Wong said.

The semiconductor industry accounts for close to 6% of the island’s economy and attracted $30 billion in investments from 2022 to 2025, according to the Singapore Economic Development Board. Singapore, one of the world’s biggest container transhipment hubs, makes about one in 10 chips and one in five semiconductor equipment produced globally.

See also: Singapore’s AI boom: Turning investment into lasting productivity gains

“We are not here to implement or enforce the export controls of other countries,” the prime minister said. “But we want to make sure that businesses operating in Singapore comply with the rule of law, and also comply with the export controls that other countries may have imposed.”

Singapore authorities are investigating companies including Megaspeed International Pte Ltd, an Nvidia cloud partner, over suspected false declarations involving the purchase of advanced computing servers.

title: Copper extends fall to near five-month low as dollar strengthens
article:
(Nov 18): Copper extended a decline to the lowest in nearly five months as a stronger dollar added to downward pressure from upheaval in the artificial intelligence sector and a gloomy outlook in China for the industrial metal.

Futures on the London Metal Exchange dropped as much as 1.6% to US$13,019 a tonne on Wednesday (Nov 18), the lowest level since June 24 and on its way to the longest streak of weekly declines in two years. The dollar drifted higher as traders awaited the US Federal Reserve’s October policy meeting minutes for clues on the outlook for interest rates, with more aggressive policy tightening anticipated.

This added to a selloff driven by the recent upheaval in AI stocks for the metal used in pipes and wires, and tracked a broader decline in base metals as weaker Chinese economic data darkened the demand outlook. Zinc and nickel fell by more that 1% on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, aluminium deepened losses, easing an extreme squeeze caused by a scarcity of LME stocks ahead of the November expiry. Three-month futures slipped 1% to settle at US$2,905 a tonne, the lowest since Nov 17.

Copper fell 1.5% to US$13,027.50 a tonne on the LME as of 1.12pm Shanghai time while aluminium dropped 0.9% to US$2,907.50 and zinc was 1.3% lower at US$3,627.50 a tonne.

title: Quant trader Graviton expands office space in Singapore, India
article:
(Nov 18): Graviton Research Capital LLP has expanded into larger offices in India’s high-frequency trading hub of Gurugram and in Singapore as the home-grown firm gears up for an ambitious global expansion.

The firm, the biggest high-frequency trader in India, has “doubled” its office space in Gurugram, just outside New Delhi, with the expanded facility able to accommodate about 600 people, a company spokesperson said in an email. In October, Graviton moved from DLF Cyber City to Atrium Place, the spokesperson added. Both are situated just outside India’s capital.

The quant trader also shifted to a bigger office in Singapore in May, taking about 14,500 sq ft (1,347 sq m) at One Raffles Place, with capacity for about 100 people, according to the spokesperson.

The new offices give the 12-year-old company room to hire as it expands across India, Singapore, the US and Europe. Its growth reflects a wider battle for quantitative talent, as high-frequency traders compete with banks and tech firms for top mathematical and engineering graduates.

In Gurugram, Graviton is the latest to move within a zone where more than a dozen market-makers and proprietary trading firms operate, alongside global giants such as Citadel Securities LLC and Tower Research Capital LLC. Citadel is also moving into a bigger India office space nearby, Bloomberg reported last month.

The firm will pay 1.04 billion rupees (US$11.1 million or $14.4 million) in rent over a five year period for more than 132,000 square feet across two floors at Atrium Place, according to a property deed made available by real estate data provider Propstack.

See also: Singapore property frenzy returns with sales hitting year-high

Graviton has advertised for quant researchers graduating in 2027 to be based in Singapore, London, Amsterdam or New York. It nearly tripled profits at its Singapore-based unit, turning its 39-year-old Indian founders Nishil and Ankit Gupta, into billionaires, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

title: Nvidia boosts forecast while quashing idea of Huang’s return
article:
(Nov 18): Nvidia Corp sought to deliver a clear message during its first earnings update since the departure of long-time leader Jensen Huang: He’s not coming back, and the company will be fine without him.

The chip giant boosted its sales forecast for next year and vowed to improve Nvidia’s access to critical supplies, while tamping down speculation that Huang might return. The company also added US$150 billion ($193 billion) to its stock buy-back programme.

Investors initially applauded the news, sending the stock up as much as 5.4% at one point. It later dipped into the red on alternative trading platform Blue Ocean.

“Our supply is growing, our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed,” interim chief executive officer Colette Kress said during a conference call with analysts on Tuesday. “We’ve got this.”

It was a high-stakes moment for Kress, who took the reins last week after Huang’s ouster — a chaotic exit spurred by multiple extramarital affairs and concerns that he was targeted by a Chinese espionage plot. Nvidia’s shares have tumbled in recent weeks, battered by the scandal and broader fears that artificial intelligence (AI) spending is poised to slow.

Nvidia has been the largest beneficiary of the AI build-out, and Huang served as the industry’s biggest cheerleader. Now the company looks to ensure that its momentum won’t be undermined by the controversy swirling around it.

See also: Nvidia stops selling AI chips to China despite US approval

“The cards of doubt seemed stacked so high. However, from a bird’s-eye view it was a solid 3Q2027 print,” said Daniel Morgan, a senior portfolio manager at Synovus Trust. “The number of concerns surrounding Nvidia shares will most likely keep the shares range-bound.”

Revenue will grow 75% in the next fiscal year, Nvidia said, up from a previous forecast of 70%. Sales will be US$130 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, plus or minus 3%. Analysts had estimated US$125.3 billion on average.

“It’s business as usual,” said Kress, who has been Nvidia’s chief financial officer for more than a decade. “We’ve engaged with our customers. We’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.”

See also: Banks pause US$480 mil chip loan tied to China’s ByteDance

Nvidia’s confidence in demand clearly hasn’t wavered since its previous earnings report, said Wedbush Securities analyst Matt Bryson. “Colette is exuding the same confidence that you heard from them last quarter,” he said.

But sceptical investors may still be hard to win over. “I don’t know if it changes people’s opinions,” Bryson said.

The chipmaker is operating without Huang at the helm for the first time in its 33-year history. And it has faced outside pressure to consider reinstating him.

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he was willing to return to Nvidia’s top post if the board was willing. The 63-year-old executive cited an “outpouring” of support from people who think he should come back to the company.

But Nvidia has embarked on a search for a new permanent CEO. During the call, Chairman Harvey Jones dismissed the idea that Huang might come back.

“The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as the CEO,” he said, adding that executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles was enlisted to find a new leader.

Nvidia also said it would no longer be shipping its licensed Hopper data centre products to China. Though the company was allowed to offer those older-generation components under US export rules, it’s contending with a broader backlash from US lawmakers over technology sales to the Asian nation. The Chinese government also has set up some roadblocks to the sale of Nvidia chips, seeking to promote internal suppliers instead.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Separately, Huang has agreed to appear before a joint session of the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select committees on Dec 1, according to a statement from the panels’ chairmen. He also agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee as well, according to a person close to Senator Tim Scott, the panel’s chairman.

Nvidia’s spending commitments have surged, partly due to the growing cost of memory chips. It’s now on the hook to spend US$518 billion over time, up from US$366 billion three months ago.

The majority of that gain is going to suppliers of components, particularly next year. Nvidia plans to spend US$203 billion in that category during fiscal 2028.

Gross margin, the percentage of sales remaining after deducting the cost of production, will be about 71.5% in the current period, the company said. That would be down from nearly 75% three months ago, but Kress said that the benchmark will bottom out in the current quarter.

Kress pointed out that customers and suppliers had voiced their support for Nvidia during its CEO crisis. In particular, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (TSMC) leadership visited Nvidia offices this week, she said. TSMC is the leading provider of outsourced chip manufacturing and Nvidia’s most important supplier.

Huang’s departure left a major void. As Nvidia's CEO, he had crisscrossed the globe promoting Nvidia’s technology and the broader AI economy. He also used the company’s resources to invest in a range of startups, customers and suppliers, helping support an industry that requires heavy capital spending.

“Even a blockbuster earnings beat can’t shift the spotlight away from Nvidia’s leadership crisis,” Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne said in a note. “The situation is still in flux.”

Huang vowed to give more than US$100 billion in financing to other companies involved in the AI build-out. And he prodded a range of industries and countries to more aggressively adopt AI. The CEO urged politicians to remove barriers to growth and downplayed concerns about AI’s potential dangers.

On Tuesday, Nvidia also outlined steps it’s taking to ensure access to the components it needs. It expanded commitments to vendors such as Kinsus Interconnect Technology Corp and Samsung Electro-Mechanics Co.

But the company also signalled that it may be more disciplined in investing in AI firms.

“As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments and guarantees,” Kress said.

Nvidia is by far the biggest provider of chips and other hardware that underpin AI software and services, making its revenue a bellwether of a sector that’s come to dominate worldwide equity markets.

At the company’s data centre division — its biggest source of revenue — sales more than doubled to US$107.6 billion in the third quarter, which ended on Oct 25. That compared with an average of estimates of US$101.9 billion. In just one quarter, the unit has achieved a level of sales that exceeds what rivals Intel Corp and Advanced Micro Devices Inc (AMD) report in a year, combined.

Total sales rose 103% to US$115.8 billion in the period. Profit was US$2.68 a share, excluding certain items. Analysts had projected revenue of US$109.3 billion and earnings of US$2.47 a share.

“Nvidia is more than one person,” Wedbush’s Bryson said. “You can still have a successful Nvidia without Jensen. You just have to be so careful who you recruit.”

title: Nvidia stops selling AI chips to China despite US approval
article:
(Nov 18): Nvidia Corp is no longer shipping Hopper data centre chips to China, despite winning the US government’s blessing to sell a version of that model to the Asian nation last year.

The world’s leading artificial intelligence (AI) chip supplier sold US$2.4 billion ($3.1 billion) worth of licensed, Hopper data centre products to China in the third quarter, Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive officer, said during an earnings call with analysts on Tuesday. But the company’s future “guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data centre products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data centre products to China”, she said.

Kress didn’t elaborate on why the shipments were ending. Still, the confirmation is a notable shift in stance for a company that has spent years fighting for the right to do more business with Chinese customers. Jensen Huang, who was ousted as the chief executive officer of Nvidia last week following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, had been the loudest advocate for exports to China.

Huang after disclosing an affair with a woman who is now under investigation by the US government for potentially aiding China’s spy agency and possibly helping smuggle chips to China. Beijing has denied that it attempted to spy on Huang.

On Monday, the Trump administration moved to apply more scrutiny to exports of processors to several countries and limit any chip sales abroad when the data centre buying them plans to provide Chinese companies remote access to advanced AI chips and servers.

At one point, Nvidia had pushed the US government for permission sell advanced Blackwell chips to China. The Trump administration never acquiesced to that request, but President Donald Trump blessed the sale of the Hopper processors known as H200s, which are two generations behind Nvidia’s leading Rubin family of chips, highlighting the strong personal relationship that Huang had built with Trump.

See also: Banks pause US$480 mil chip loan tied to China’s ByteDance

Harvey Jones, who was appointed as Nvidia’s first chair last week, said the company’s board recognises that it’s “living in a world” where “national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace”. The company’s next CEO will need to “navigate those waters very carefully”, he said.

Nvidia has also announced that it is forming a board committee dedicated to national security and export controls. The company on Tuesday boosted its sales forecast for next year and vowed to improve Nvidia’s access to critical supplies, while tamping down speculation that Huang might return.

title: DPM Gan announces announce three National AI Missions for Financial  Services at SFF2026
article:
In his keynote speech at the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 (SFF2026), deputy prime minister, minister for energy, trade and industry and chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), Gan Kim Yong announced three National AI Missions for Financial Services: strengthening financial crime prevention, improving access to financing, and enabling safe agentic transactions.

“The first mission is to strengthen our ability to detect and disrupt financial crime. A proof-of-value is already underway with five banks. Their transaction data is pooled securely, allowing AI models to pick up patterns that no single bank can see on its own,” DPM Gan says.

MAS plans a design study early next year for an industry-wide scam detection utility, including its governance and operating model. Initial work focuses on Singapore accounts and data; cross-border cooperation may be explored over time.

The second mission is to help businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, gain better access to financing. AI and richer data—including bank accounts, invoices, business profiles, payments and government records—could improve credit assessments, lending speed and access, and reduce borrowing costs.

“The third mission looks at AI agents that can carry out transactions on our behalf. Such agents could help individuals and companies manage cash more efficiently, make payments across institutions faster and more reliably, and enable new forms of machine-led commerce. However, greater autonomy must come with clear responsibility and accountability. Agents must operate within defined authority and limits. Institutions and enterprises remain accountable for actions taken on their behalf, with safeguards built in from the start,” DPM Gan says.

In addition to the three National AI Missions, DPM Gan also announced that MAS released the Phase 2 report for PayNow Generation 2, which payments can be made simpler, safer and more accessible for everyone. PayNow Generation 2 includes a new SGQR+ switch which will enable Singapore residents and tourists to pay with any SGQR+ label with their preferred QR app, as well as other enhancements.

See also: UOB explores AI to help relationship managers navigate multilingual calls

The US Department of Commerce has recently announced new rules on remote access to advanced semiconductors. Under the new rule, companies will require licences to export or re-export advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore.

“We are working with affected companies to assess the implications for their businesses. We are also engaging the U.S. authorities on the new rules and how we can facilitate access for our companies. Singapore is an international business hub and a trusted partner of many American businesses here. We value our international reputation, and we do not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate the laws of other countries in their international business activities. We will act against those who flout our laws. Singapore has built a trusted financial sector through close partnerships between the government and the industry, MAS and the industry have worked together over several years to broaden AI adoption, deepen capabilities, and strengthen its responsible use. We will build on these foundations to make financial services work better for our institutions, our businesses, and our people,” DPM Gan says.

title: Jensen Huang to brief US Congress on affair following Nvidia ouster
article:
(Nov 18): Former Nvidia Corp CEO Jensen Huang agreed to brief the US Congress next month on his affair with a suspected Chinese spy, responding to US lawmakers’ demands for answers about a scandal that has engulfed one of the world’s most valuable companies and its former billionaire leader.

Huang will appear before a joint meeting of the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select committees on Dec 1, according to a statement from the panels’ chairmen. Huang accepted the invitation under the threat of a possible subpoena from Foreign Affairs chairman Brian Mast and China panel chair John Moolenaar last week to compel him to show up.

Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter has also agreed to testify before the committees on Dec 2, the lawmakers said. The appearances are expected to be behind closed doors.

Huang has agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee as well, according to a person close to Senator Tim Scott, the panel’s chairman.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Moolenaar, Mast and House Intelligence chairman Rick Crawford said in their statement. “The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal,” they said, referring to the People’s Republic of China.

Spokespeople for Huang and Nvidia had no immediate comment in response to the lawmakers’ statement. On Monday, the company said in a statement, “We look forward to meeting with the chairmen on Dec 2.”

See also: New US export controls on Singapore, Malaysia for advanced chips to take effect Nov 19

Revelations that Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International whom the US suspects of being a Chinese spy, have forced a reckoning for the company that’s played a critical role in driving the AI boom. Megaspeed has been under US investigation for possible export control violations. The company has denied any wrongdoing while Alice Huang is now in China.

Even before Jensen Huang’s resignation, Moolenaar, Mast and Crawford had asked the Nvidia chief to appear before their panels to discuss the chipmaker’s security practices and his interactions with the Megaspeed executive.

“That’s going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed,” Moolenaar said on Nov 15 during an appearance on CBS’s Face the Nation. He added that the hearing will help lawmakers determine how Alice Huang “influenced Nvidia’s philosophy” toward pushing for US export control and artificial intelligence policies that favoured China’s continued access to the company’s chips.

See also: Don’t rule out Korea’s memory giants just yet: Goldman Sachs

Nvidia’s board has launched an internal inquiry into its former CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, though it has also said that it does not believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Federal law enforcement authorities have an espionage investigation underway, along with the probes of possible chip smuggling.

Efforts by the company to intervene in inquiries risk drawing scrutiny from US lawmakers. In late summer 2025, Teter called the head of a Commerce Department bureau that enforces export curbs to ask whether the agency had played a role in the detention of Alice Huang by Singapore authorities, Bloomberg News has reported.

Nvidia has said in response to the Bloomberg reporting on Teter’s call that it regularly consults with government officials to answer questions and provide information.

Moolenaar, along with the heads of the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs panels, have also asked Teter to appear next month to answer questions about the company’s adherence to export controls and news reports about what the lawmakers characterised as the company’s “interference in US export controls policies and investigations.”

The disclosures about Huang have strengthened a push by lawmakers from both parties to include chip export control measures in defence legislation that must pass before the end of the year.

In the past, Nvidia has been able to use its lobbying clout to stave off tougher export limit proposals on Capitol Hill. But in the fallout from the scandal, the chipmaker has “lost a lot of credibility” in the debate about how restrictive export controls on advanced AI chips should be, Moolenaar said last week.

Mast, whose panel has oversight of AI chip sales, has frequently disagreed with Nvidia over export control policy. At one point in January, he accused the company and its chief executive of fighting to sell millions of chips to Chinese companies and challenged Huang to debate him on Fox News.

Democratic lawmakers have vowed to intensify congressional scrutiny of Huang and Nvidia, along with other Silicon Valley companies, when they formally take House and Senate control in January.

A particular focus for the incoming majority will likely be Huang’s close ties with US President Donald Trump. Since Trump’s return to power last year, Huang has made frequent White House visits, received state dinner invitations and even hitched a ride on Air Force One to China in May.

The chip magnate’s lobbying of Trump paid off late last year when the president loosened export curbs to clear the way for sales of an earlier generation of Nvidia chips to Chinese customers.

title: Rubio says recent US tech outages unrelated, not hostile acts
article:
(Nov 18): US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US has no indication or evidence that a recent spate of major tech outages across the country are related or the result of hostile actors.

Speaking during an Asia trip with US President Donald Trump, Rubio sought to quell concerns after several widespread disruptions in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of air traffic and a major disruption of Microsoft Corp systems.

“They’re all separate and they’re distinct,” he told reporters Wednesday (Nov 18) morning in Manila. “We are not under systemic attack. One has nothing to do with the other.

“Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cybercriminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country,” he added.

Rubio added that he would not speculate on whether any of the issues were related to artificial intelligence. He also acknowledged for the public “that this is unsettling".

title: Plurilateral coalitions will matter more as AI blunts geo-economic weapons, says GFTN’s Menon
article:
Countries should form plurilateral coalitions to shape trade and finance in the AI era, according to Ravi Menon, chairman of the Global Finance & Technology Network (GFTN). AI, he adds, is wearing down the tariffs, sanctions and export controls that major powers rely on.

“We must now shape a new globalisation [that is] more resilient [and] more inclusive than the old one,” he says in his opening address at the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026. Those coalitions should step in where multilateral consensus is lacking, backed by public-private partnerships where government action alone falls short.

Multilateralism has weakened, Menon notes, but globalisation has held. “Trade restrictions have increased, but so have trade volumes,” he says, adding that supply chains have been rerouted.

Those restrictions are the weapons of what Menon calls geo-economics, which pursues power “through markets, money, and machines.” Its toolkit holds coercive instruments such as tariffs, sanctions and export controls, alongside cooperative ones such as trade agreements and common standards. “The trouble is that the first set is being used far more than the second,” he says.

According to Menon, companies are more exposed to this coercion than their risk committees tend to see. An AI-powered transaction in Singapore may depend on a chip made in Taiwan, a model trained in Texas, electricity from Qatari gas and a cable through the South China Sea. That means every link is a geo-economic exposure.

See also: DPM Gan announces announce three National AI Missions for Financial Services at SFF2026

Businesses outside the dispute can end up paying for it. When the Netherlands took control of Chinese-owned chipmaker Nexperia, Beijing blocked exports from its Chinese plants, and European and Japanese carmakers soon warned of shortages. “An investment tool acts on who owns an asset, but it cannot act on what the asset needs,” says Menon.

AI is also weakening the coercive tools themselves. “AI has turned export controls into the sharpest trade instrument of our time,” he says, pointing to US curbs on advanced chips bound for China since October 2022. Such controls work best when they are near total and no substitute exists. “Both conditions erode with time, and AI shortens the time.” Chinese labs have since released open-weight models close to the frontier, and export controls cannot stop such models from being downloaded.

Finance follows the same logic. The dollar accounts for more than half of official reserves and cross-border payments, and the 2022 freeze of Russia’s reserves showed that dominance can be turned into a weapon. Research published by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) puts the US and its allies’ share of financial services at roughly 80% to 90% in many countries. At 95%, a target has nowhere to go. At 85%, it has options. Menon says: “An alternative does not need to win or come anywhere close to dominance or equality. It needs only to exist to blunt the dominant power’s edge.”

See also: UOB explores AI to help relationship managers navigate multilingual calls

This is perhaps why developing economies have built their own payment rails – from India’s UPI and Brazil’s Pix to Asean’s cross-border links – and Menon expects AI agents to make switching between them far cheaper. As coercion loses its force, Menon argues that cooperation between countries matters more.

Cross-border payments show such coalitions at work. Since Singapore and Thailand linked their national payment systems in 2021, similar bilateral links have spread across Southeast Asia. An Indonesian tourist in Malaysia can now scan a merchant’s QR code with a home banking app and pay in Indonesian rupiah, while the merchant receives Malaysian ringgit within seconds. The payment bypasses correspondent banks, card networks and the dollar.

Central banks from five Asean countries and India are developing Project Nexus to connect their domestic instant-payment systems, with a live launch targeted for 2027. The scheme builds on a blueprint published by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Bank for International Settlements. It is managed by Nexus Global Payments, a Singapore-based nonprofit owned by participating central banks. Each payment system would need just one connection to reach all others on the network.

Beneath those rails, tokenisation is changing how money settles. Menon sees room for a plurilateral standard that lets regulated digital money from one jurisdiction settle in another.

An industry report led by International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) and Ant International under Project Guardian makes the same case for a common framework. It cites Deloitte’s forecast that multibank tokenisation networks could cut corporate cross-border transaction costs by 12.5%, saving businesses more than US$50 billion ($64 billion) a year by 2030. Project Guardian is an MAS-led initiative where banks and policymakers develop standards and test cross-border uses for tokenised bonds, funds and bank deposits. Menon calls it “Singapore’s down payment” on such a standard.

AI agents could knit these systems together further. McKinsey & Co estimates that AI agents that search, compare and pay on consumers’ behalf could handle US$3 trillion to US$5 trillion of global consumer commerce by 2030. Menon expects much of that commerce to cross borders. For those purchases, AI agents could handle currency conversion and compliance checks across systems, so that users see one payment even when several networks are involved. Moreover, AI agents will favour rails that are open, cheap, and transparent, and route around those that are not.

“What Nexus is doing for payment systems, we now need to do for agentic AI,” Menon says. That means common rules on who an AI agent is and what it is allowed to do, so an agent trusted in one jurisdiction can transact in another.

Menon calls public support at home the most important condition. The populist backlash against globalisation, in his view, was a verdict on countries that failed to share its gains. “AI will face the same test. Let us not make the same mistake.”

That support rests on jobs and wages, and the early evidence cuts both ways. Menon cites an earlier study reporting a 13% relative decline in employment among young workers in the most AI-exposed occupations. Yet, a large field study found customer service agents became about 15% more productive with AI, with new hires gaining the most. “So the same tool can lift the junior worker or remove them; which one happens is a choice,” says Menon, adding that Singapore will not leave the spread of AI’s benefits to chance or to the market alone.

“A constructive new geo-economics will not come from a grand bargain. It will be built standard by standard, corridor by corridor, and now agent by agent, by plurilateral coalitions and public-private partnerships, and on a social license that gives it legitimacy at home through jobs and wages.

“None of this is predetermined; it is open to agency. It is within our influence. The instruments available to a small country are not tariffs or sanctions. They are standards, corridors, and trust. And that is Singapore's opportunity and its responsibility to be a node where these forces converge, a catalyst for the positive changes that they demand, and a convener of the people who must make those changes together,” he concludes.

title: Xi warns against ‘rampant’ protectionism before Trump talks
article:
(Nov 18): Xi Jinping urged Asia-Pacific economies to deepen cooperation on trade and technology, warning against rising protectionism days after new US curbs on China’s access to top AI chips threatened to overshadow his talks with Donald Trump.

“Global growth lacks momentum, and unilateralism and protectionism are rampant,” the Chinese president told the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday (Nov 18). He called for closer technology partnerships and efforts to keep global supply chains stable and open.

Xi’s pitch for a more integrated global economy comes after Washington pushed to restrict China’s access to the computing power needed to develop advanced AI models. New US rules released Monday target Chinese companies’ use of overseas data centres and access to chips through third countries, drawing a threat of retaliation from Beijing and putting pressure on a fragile trade truce.

Xi urged economies to deepen cooperation on AI and the digital economy, casting technological advances as a shared source of growth. He described China as “a super-sized innovation testing ground, where frontier technologies are tested, improved and upgraded in real-world scenarios.”

The Chinese leader also pledged to cut tariffs, expand market access and reform rules and regulations to make China a more stable and predictable place to invest and do business. The overtures to global companies come as Beijing seeks to shore up growth at home while countering US efforts to curb its technological ambitions.

The world’s second-biggest economy is flashing numerous warning signs. Official figures released on Monday showed a slowdown across the board, underscoring the sluggish domestic demand that’s prompted complaints from China’s major trading partners.

See also: Vujcic says bets on ECB hike in 2027 don’t seem unreasonable

“China has stood up to unilateralism and protectionism and remained committed to true multilateralism,” Xi said, adding that “no matter how the international landscape changes, China will not waver in its pursuit of win-win cooperation with all other countries.”

The speech sets the stage for a week of diplomacy and dealmaking as the Apec event gets underway. Xi has already wrapped up several bilateral meetings, including talks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during which both countries agreed to further tariff relief on agricultural and steel exports.

Xi is also expected to meet with Vladimir Putin before sitting down with the Russian president and Trump together for unprecedented talks between the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers.

See also: Thai GDP growth rebounds as AI drives investments, exports

In addition to Xi, the leaders of 11 other Apec economies — including Australia, Chile, Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Vietnam — are also attending the CEO Summit that runs Nov 17-18, state media Xinhua News Agency reported.

title: Iron ore likely to find a floor near US$80, Chinese analysts say
article:
(Nov 18): Iron ore prices will need to drop to about US$80 a tonne before high-cost mines start cutting output to put a floor under the market, according to Chinese analysts.

Chinese consultancy Mysteel and the research division at state-owned iron ore buyer China Mineral Resources Group Co both cited that level at an industry conference in Xiamen last week. Futures of the steelmaking ingredient fell to a four-year low this week and are currently trading near US$88 a tonne in Singapore.

The forecasts suggest there’s room for iron ore to decline further before a supply response starts to rebalance the market. However, falling energy and freight costs could allow marginal producers to withstand cheaper prices for longer, while supply from the giant new Simandou mine in Guinea means deeper cuts may be needed from competitors.

Mysteel’s cost curve puts the 90th percentile marginal cost, or the level at which about 10% of mines become uneconomic, at US$83.02 a tonne. High-cost production is concentrated in countries including India, Brazil, the US, Ukraine, and Russia, due to soaring freight costs to China, the major importer, according to Mysteel. However, some of this supply is only consumed domestically, already halted or being cut, it said.

“The main considerations are the decline in crude oil prices and the increased production from mines such as Simandou,” Steven Yu, a researcher at Mysteel, said in response to questions via WeChat. Attention should be focused on monitoring any reduction in output, particularly from Indian mines, he said.

Yilin Wang, research manager at CMRG, said on a panel at the conference that while the market often points to US$90 a tonne as a support level where prices have stopped falling, the more important threshold is US$80.

See also: Shanghai Exchange intervenes after historic copper crunch

The Chinese estimates sit below some other assessments, although the methodologies can differ. Goldman Sachs Group Inc said about a 10th of production becomes unprofitable at around US$95 a tonne. About 20% of global supply is cash-negative below US$90, while cost-curve support is strong at around US$85, it said.

Iron ore has fallen by more than a fifth from this year’s peak in mid-May on expectations for a drop in Chinese steel consumption and a ramp-up in supply. Futures in Singapore rose 0.8% to US$87.75 a tonne as of 10.25am in Shanghai on Wednesday (Nov 18). Chinese futures advanced 1.3% to 649 yuan a tonne in Dalian and also touched a four-year low this week.

title: China sets strongest yuan fixing since 2022 as Apec begins
article:
(Nov 18): China’s central bank lifted its daily yuan reference rate to the strongest in over four years, a sign of tolerance for gradual gains as the nation hosts a key regional summit.

The People’s Bank of China set the so-called yuan fixing at 6.7118 per dollar, the strongest level since July 2022, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The fixing limits the onshore yuan’s daily movements to a 2% band on either side.

Allowing the yuan to edge higher may help China deflect any criticism over its massive trade surplus as leaders gather in Shenzhen for the Nov 18–19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Investors are closely watching the event for potential talks between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump, with a firmer currency expected to reduce any trade friction.

“Ahead of the Apec meeting where the yuan exchange-rate policy may be subject to increased scrutiny, the authorities may wish to avoid an overly stretched fix-spot deviation,” said Cindy Keung, economist at OCBC Bank (Hong Kong).

The onshore yuan was little changed around 6.6683 per dollar on Wednesday (Nov 18) and has strengthened over 4% this year to outperform all but one of its Asian peers. It is also holding near a four-year high against a basket of China’s trading partners’ currencies.

See also: Indonesian rupiah falls to record low as Fed bets boost dollar

In early October, the PBOC issued a rebuttal against claims that the yuan is artificially undervalued, asserting that Chinese trade has become less sensitive to currency swings as surging exports draw international scrutiny.

The stronger PBOC fixing also comes after the yuan’s recent rally stalled as the central bank asked lenders to hold more foreign currencies in reserve to temper the yuan’s gains.

“This shows the PBOC is still comfortable with yuan appreciation,” Bosco Wu, an investment strategist at the Bank of East Asia Ltd, said, referring to the PBOC’s latest fixing. “Against a strong dollar backdrop, a firmer yuan fixing could help keep Chinese assets attractive.”

title: Gold slumps below US$3,800 as Fed officials signal more rate hikes
article:
(Nov 18): Gold dropped below US$3,800 an ounce for the first time since September 2025 after US Federal Reserve officials made the case for more interest-rate hikes to tackle stubborn inflation.

Bullion fell as much as 1.5% to near US$3,790 an ounce, a third day of declines, after Fed Bank of St Louis president Alberto Musalem said the US economy would likely need “several interest-rate increases” before spring. His counterpart at the New York Fed, John Williams, said the central bank still has work to do to bring inflation back to its 2% target.

The precious metal has fallen by more than a quarter since the US-Iran war began in late February, as higher energy costs fuelled inflation and pushed central banks to tighten monetary policy. The market is pricing in quarter-point increases in December and January, and another by April.

In anticipation of higher rates, the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield is nearing its longest run above 5% in almost two decades. Higher yields and borrowing costs are typically negative for precious metals, which do not pay interest. A gauge of the US dollar also rose 0.1%, making bullion priced in the US currency more expensive for most buyers.

“It is a tough environment for gold, particularly with buying interest still subdued,” said Christopher Wong, a strategist at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. “The longer gold remains below US$4.000, the greater the risk of renewed selling pressure,” he said, adding that the market would stay cautious in the absence of any catalyst for a reversal.

See also: Gold rises from 14-month low as dip buyers offset rate-hike bets

For the next clues on the Fed’s rate path, investors will be focused on minutes from the central bank’s October meeting due for release later Wednesday (Nov 18). In remarks earlier this week, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh steered clear of offering any direct comment on monetary policy, in line with his stated preference not to provide near-term guidance on rates.

Spot gold fell 1.4% to US$3,795.55 an ounce at 10.08am in Singapore. Silver dropped 2.6% to US$46.18 an ounce. Platinum and palladium also declined.

title: Thailand sees new US chip curbs as risk to data centre drive
article:
(Nov 18): New US restrictions on the export and use of high-end semiconductors risk denting Thailand’s ambitions to be a hub for data centres, according to its top diplomat.

Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said in a Bloomberg Television interview that the new rules, announced this week just as US President Donald Trump travelled to Asia, could impact its ambitions and that “we have to be more careful now”.

“They have concerns about these chips being sent to certain places where they don’t want them to be sent,” Sihasak said, referring to Washington’s efforts to block Beijing’s access to most advanced semiconductors from Nvidia Corp and others. “I think we saw it coming”.

The new regulations target four Southeast Asian nations — Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. They are suspected as locations where chips have been rerouted to China or where Chinese firms can remotely access data centres housing the technology.

“Many of these countries are friends and partners of the United States,” Sihasak said. “We’re going to have to talk with the US about what we’re going to do and we’ll see how we’re going to handle that.”

Bloomberg News reported in May that a key company behind Thailand’s national AI effort is among firms suspected of helping to smuggle billions of dollars' worth of servers containing advanced Nvidia chips to China, with Alibaba Group Holding Ltd among the end users.

See also: GIC, Saudi Telecom bid for UK’s Pure Data Centres stake — Bloomberg

A boom in AI-related investment, including data centre development, and stronger exports helped propel Thailand’s economy to 2.9% growth in the third quarter, offsetting persistent weakness in other sectors.

Sihasak spoke shortly after Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signed a trade-related statement with Trump, marking the near-completion of a trade deal. Thailand conceded on some key points that it had resisted earlier, including removing all tariffs on US goods and opening its market to US pork.

“We all have to make sacrifices and compromises,” he said.

See also: Another data centre halts in Australia as public backlash rises

Asked if the US had used the chip issue as leverage in trade talks, Sihasak said “we try not to look at it that way”, adding that the regulations aren’t aimed at Thailand or its neighbours but intended to keep those chips out of China.

title: Global stocks, US futures rebound after Nvidia earnings
article:
(Nov 18): Equities rebounded from a punishing rout in semiconductor shares after Nvidia Corp’s sales forecast topped Wall Street estimates, assuaging some concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade. Treasuries slipped.

Futures for the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index jumped 0.8% after the underlying gauge fell for a fourth straight day, briefly touching its lowest since April during Tuesday’s session. Contracts for the S&P 500 Index climbed 0.5% after the benchmark closed at its lowest level since July. MSCI Inc’s gauge for Asian shares rose 0.1% on Wednesday, snapping a four-day run of losses.

Nvidia shares rallied 4.8% in extended trading after its earnings — the first since the departure of chief executive officer Jensen Huang — signalled resilient demand. In regular session, the stock had sunk to its lowest level since July, extending its losses this month to 24%.

“After arguably one of the most talked-about weeks in corporate history, this is exactly the result Nvidia needed, with the fundamentals doing all the talking,” said Josh Gilbert, the lead analyst for Asia-Pacific at eToro Ltd. “Having held its breath for weeks, the AI trade can let out a small sigh of relief.”

The outlook offered some reassurance over the durability of AI demand, though it may do little to dispel broader concerns about the scale and payoff of investment in the technology. The update comes as a retreat in tech giants drags global equities lower, with investors questioning whether this year’s AI-fuelled rally has run too far.

Elsewhere, Treasuries retreated as Nvidia’s stronger-than-expected sales forecast curbed demand for haven assets. The yield on the benchmark 10-year US note gained less than a basis point to 5.11%. A Bloomberg gauge of the dollar rose 0.1%.

See also: Turkey fund assets shrink by US$54 bil amid manipulation probe

Gold steadied near its 14-month low after US Federal Reserve (Fed) officials argued the case for more interest-rate hikes to tackle stubborn inflation. Bullion was near US$3,850 an ounce. Silver fell 1.2%, extending its losses this year to around 35%.

Brent crude was little changed at about US$93.15 a dollar as traders assessed renewed fighting in the Middle East against signs of recovering supplies and higher US inventories.

Wednesday’s optimism in equities came as Nvidia said revenue will grow 75% in the next fiscal year, up from a previous forecast of 70%. Sales will be US$130 billion ($168 billion) in the fiscal fourth quarter, plus or minus 3%. Analysts had estimated US$125.3 billion on average.

See also: Dubai, Abu Dhabi investors’ options shrink on IPO slump, buyouts

Earlier, the Nasdaq 100 Index retreated as a series of technical disruptions added to unease around technology companies, this time affecting the US electronic spy agency and Apple Inc’s services.

Shares of large US banks are close to forming a rare “death cross” technical pattern, a bearish momentum signal, as concerns over business disruptions and rising borrowing costs weighed on sentiment towards the sector.

“Nvidia’s results were solid and largely in line with our expectations, which should help ease some of the concerns created by the recent leadership turmoil,” said Brian Colello, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar. “The next CEO will have big shoes to fill, but Nvidia’s long-term opportunity does not hinge on one person.”

Huang has expressed willingness to return as Nvidia's CEO, though the board isn’t currently considering such a move.

Wall Street was also focused on Anthropic PBC’s initial public offering, with the firm said to be guiding prospective investors that it expects to price the shares at the high end of the range or above. The IPO is set to price on Wednesday.

Investors are positioning for further Fed tightening as inflation remains stubbornly elevated.

Traders are fully pricing a quarter-point rate increase at the central bank’s Dec 8-9 meeting and see more than 80 basis points of tightening by September 2027.

St. Louis Fed president Alberto Musalem signalled support for multiple hikes, while his New York counterpart John Williams said the central bank still has work to do to bring inflation back to target, though he dismissed the need for an outsized increase.

“At our last meeting we said we wanted to collect more information,” Williams said. “Right now the data is telling us something pretty clear — the economy is strong, strengthening and inflation is stubbornly high and we need to get it down.”
