title: Banks pause US$480 mil chip loan tied to China’s ByteDance
article:
(Nov 18): Bankers have frozen work on a US$480 million loan that would have funded advanced Nvidia Corp chips for use by China’s ByteDance, according to people familiar with the matter.

After the US placed its latest curbs on access to AI chips, bankers at five lenders evaluating the deal have had internal discussions about pulling out or not joining the loan amid fears of violating the new restrictions, the people said.

Singapore-based neocloud Aolani Cloud Pte recently began inviting banks to join the loan, which would fund the purchase of GPUs for a data centre in Malaysia. But on Monday, the US announced a rule requiring data centre operators in countries including Singapore and Malaysia to get a licence to buy advanced AI chips. The step is aimed at curbing Chinese companies’ remote access to such technology, which is how TikTok parent ByteDance would use the Nvidia GPUs.

The pause in work on the loan illustrates how the Trump administration’s surprise move has caught many dealmakers in Asia off-guard. Across the region, lenders scrambled on Tuesday to work out what the new regulations would mean for billions of AI debt in the pipeline and deals that have already been done.

“We have spent significant time with our banking and financing partners to assess and anticipate regulatory risk ahead of this recent new ruling,” a spokesperson for Aolani said in response to questions about the loan being paused. “We are pro-actively working with regulators and our financing partners to ensure the project delivery goes ahead in full compliance with the new ruling.”

DBS Group Holdings Ltd, which is the mandated lead arranger and book-runner on the deal, declined to comment.

See also: Nvidia stops selling AI chips to China despite US approval

It is not yet clear how exactly the licence approval process will work and which firms will be required to apply for them. That has prompted a barrage of questions from potential lenders, one of the people said.

It is unlikely that there would be progress on funding the Aolani deal until bankers can fully evaluate the new rule, the people said. Internally, some bankers have described the facility as dead given the risks banks could incur if it was found to violate the new US rule, they said.

title: Ambani seeks to build satellite capacity for Starlink challenge
article:
(Nov 18): Billionaire Mukesh Ambani-led Reliance Group is exploring manufacturing partnerships to support its planned 1,600-satellite broadband constellation, people familiar with the matter said, in a push to create an Indian-controlled alternative to Elon Musk’s Starlink.

The aim for a low-earth orbit network by 2035 is intended to support the growth of newly listed unit Jio Platforms Ltd, the people said, asking not to be identified because the plans are private. Reliance is in talks with Indian satellite manufacturers, technology startups and larger industrial groups on potential partnerships, offering to fund the required infrastructure.

The project underscores the challenge facing India’s space ambitions: matching strategic objectives with the manufacturing and launch capacity needed to execute them. India currently produces fewer than 15 satellites a year, according to the people, while the proposed constellation would require an output of roughly 200 satellites annually, putting Reliance at the centre of efforts to close that gap.

The approach mirrors New Delhi’s push to use the private sector to build strategic capabilities, with the Tata Group investing heavily in semiconductor and electronics manufacturing under government-backed initiatives.

Reliance plans to combine domestic manufacturing with imports, including at least 400 satellites from the US, as it works toward a September 2027 test mission and a wider deployment beginning in early 2028. The constellation is now targeted for completion by 2035, later than an earlier goal of 2030, due to manufacturing and launch constraints, the people said.

The company is in discussions with two US firms regarding potential satellite procurement and is also evaluating suppliers in Europe, they said. It is not considering China as a source for its constellation plans.

See also: Simba plans board changes as spectrum breaches go uncontested

An email sent to Reliance seeking comments did not elicit any response.

The constellation is expected to compete with Starlink in India but, unlike the Musk-backed global network of more than 10,000 satellites, Reliance’s planned system is geared primarily toward meeting India’s connectivity and strategic requirements.

See also: TeleChoice wins new $1.3 bil contract from U Mobile

Reliance intends to use the network primarily to improve connectivity across India, though the capability could also serve strategic communication needs during periods of conflict or geopolitical tensions, the people said.

Strengthening domestic space capabilities has become key for New Delhi following a recent border conflict with neighbour Pakistan and is increasing investments in surveillance satellites and partnerships with private space companies.

Industry executives say launch capacity may ultimately prove the bigger challenge. While manufacturing can be expanded with sufficient investment, deploying thousands of satellites will require a significant increase in launch frequency and access to suitable orbital slots.

“Manufacturing at scale is doable but the real challenge will be to ensure there are enough rocket launches happening in India for the satellites to be placed in the desired orbit if the constellation is planned to be implemented with Indian launch vehicles,” said Amal Chandran, CEO of satellite manufacturer HEX20.

Starlink’s entry into India meanwhile remains subject to regulatory and security scrutiny. Concerns over oversight and operational control of foreign satellite networks during periods of geopolitical tension have strengthened the case for domestically controlled alternatives.

title: Penguin denies it is in violation of UN arms embargo on Libya
article:
Penguin International disagrees with a United Nations panel that has deemed the company in violation of an international arms embargo on Libya.

According to a March 2026 report by the UN Panel of Experts on Libya, two of the vessels sold by Penguin in December 2024 to Libya, a security vessel, and a landing craft, have been classified as military equipment.

Between last January and May, Penguin was approached and corresponded with the UN Panel to provide information on those two vessels.

In the report issued by the panel in March, the security vessel was classified as a naval-type fast patrol vessel and the landing craft as a dual-use vessel, and therefore, Penguin and its subsidiary Penguin Shipyard Asia are deemed to be violation of a standing arms embargo.

However, the panel did not recommend that Penguin be sanctioned or designated as sanctioned entities by the UN.

Penguin says it was aware of the report only in September.

See also: Geo Energy confirms no new mining directive received in latest clarification statement

The company points out that the vessels were designed and built as commercial vessels and were delivered without arms or ammunition on board.

As such, it disagrees with the panel’s characterisation of the vessels and its resulting conclusion concerning the violation of arms embargo.

Citing legal advice, Penguin says the panel's report does not itself carry any direct penalties.

See also: Airwallex plans over $2 bil Singapore investment to support global growth

It is also not determinative if the UN or any of its member states will institute penalties on named persons.

Also, the naming of Penguin in the report is not itself a sanctions action and does not directly impose any UN sanctions on itself.

Last but not least, the possibility of the UN imposing sanctions against the company is "low".

Since last November, Penguin has been corresponding with Singapore Customs, which, to date, has not indicated if Penguin is in breach of Singapore laws.

Penguin is reviewing and enhancing its sanctions and export control procedures.

It is also evaluating the adequacy and effectiveness of its processes in sanctions and export-control risks and will implement such further enhancements as may be appropriate.

Meanwhile, Penguin believes there is no material disruption to its operations and is not aware if there will be a material financial impact.

"The group has never before this transaction exported any vessel to Libya and does not intend to do so in the future for as long as the (UN) Resolution is in force," says Penguin.

title: Stocks fall on tech disruptions as Nvidia in focus
article:
(Nov 18): A selloff in technology giants dragged down stocks on mounting concerns about technical disruptions, with investors also looking to Nvidia Corp.’s earnings for a read on the outlook for artificial intelligence.

In late hours, the chipmaker gave a solid revenue forecast. But a round of tech outages weighed on sentiment Tuesday, this time hitting the US electronic spy agency and Apple Inc.’s services. The S&P 500 fell to its lowest since July.

As Nvidia reports results, its long-term outlook is in question after Jensen Huang’s ouster. He expressed willingness to return as chief executive officer, but the board isn’t currently considering such an idea.

Revenue will be US$130 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, plus or minus 3%, the company said. Analysts had estimated US$125.3 billion on average. Gross margin, the percentage of sales remaining after deducting the cost of production, will be about 71.5% in the quarter.

“Investors are obviously going to want to hear a lot more about what Nvidia is going to do next and how that will impact their businesses going forward,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak.

Wall Street is also focused on Anthropic PBC’s initial public offering. The firm is said to be guiding prospective investors it expects to price the shares at the high end of the range or above. The IPO is set to price on Nov. 18.

See also: Asian stocks to fall ahead of Nvidia, Anthropic

Two of Anthropic’s biggest customers — Amazon.com Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google — are set to own nearly 15% and 14% of the firm’s outstanding capital stock respectively following the IPO and private placement.

Despite strong appetite for the sale, concerns over the payoff from hefty AI spending linger. A survey conducted by Bank of America Corp. found the share of fund managers overweight tech fell to a net 12% from 37% in October, the most since 2006.

In a bid for safety, Treasuries rose. That’s despite elevated oil prices that could make the Federal Reserve raise rates.

title: US stocks fall on tech jitters ahead of Nvidia results
article:
(Nov 18): A selloff in technology giants dragged down stocks on mounting concerns about technical disruptions, with investors also looking to Nvidia Corp’s earnings for a read on the outlook for artificial intelligence (AI).

The Nasdaq 100 fell 1.6%. Equities extended losses after CNN reported that the highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down. The chipmaker at the heart of the AI boom fell towards the lowest since June 2025. Wall Street will also be focused on Anthropic PBC’s IPO.

Nvidia formed a new board committee for oversight of national security and export control after the company became embroiled in a controversy over chip smuggling. Huang agreed to brief Congress next month on his affair with a suspected Chinese spy and the firm’s security protocols.
